title: Competing delocalisation and localisation induced by the dipolar tail in fragmented lattice gases
authors: Sabhyata Gupta, Adith Sai Aramthottil, Luis Santos
abstract: We investigate how the long-range tail of dipole-dipole interactions modifies the dynamics of strongly interacting hard-core bosons in a one-dimensional lattice. In the nearest-neighbour model, large interactions generate an emergent Hilbert-space fragmentation into manifolds labelled by the number of nearest-neighbour bonds \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\). The dipolar tail has a non-monotonic effect on this fragmented dynamics as the interaction-to-tunnelling ratio \(V/t\) is increased. At intermediate \(V/t\), it enhances delocalisation relative to the nearest-neighbour model by reducing the energetic detuning between neighbouring \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\) manifolds and sustaining their hybridisation by hopping. At larger \(V/t\), the same tail lifts degeneracies within each manifold, beginning with the splitting associated with the next-nearest-neighbour bond number \(N_{\mathrm{NNN}}\), and promotes intra-manifold localisation and Hilbert-space shattering. The competition between these two effects produces a crossover from a delocalising to a localising role of the dipolar tail, visible in the late-time spatial inhomogeneity. This crossover occurs for nearly all initial states considered and persists at different fillings. Transverse confinement strengthens the short-range part of the dipolar tail and shifts the crossover to lower \(V/t\), bringing it into the regime relevant to current experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules.
summary: This paper investigates how long-range dipolar interactions affect the dynamics of bosons in a 1D lattice, revealing a non-monotonic behavior. The dipolar tail first enhances delocalization at moderate interaction strengths by coupling different system states, but at stronger interactions, it causes localization by splitting energy degeneracies. This competition defines a critical crossover scale relevant for experiments with magnetic atoms.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the long-range dipolar tail of interactions modifies the dynamics of strongly interacting hard-core bosons in a 1D lattice, focusing on the competition between delocalization and localization.
main_result: The dipolar tail exhibits a non-monotonic effect, first enhancing delocalization at intermediate interaction strengths ($V/t$) by sustaining inter-manifold hybridization, but then promoting localization at larger $V/t$ by lifting degeneracies within manifolds.
method: The study uses real-time dynamics simulations and analyzes various diagnostics like time-averaged density inhomogeneity ($ ar{\eta}$) and the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) to quantify localization and delocalization.
model_or_system: The system is hard-core bosons on an open 1D lattice governed by a Hamiltonian including nearest-neighbor and long-range dipolar interactions ($V_r \propto 1/r^3$). The analysis compares this to a simple nearest-neighbor model.
key_observables: Time-averaged density inhomogeneity ($ ar{\eta}$), Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), and the crossover strength $(V/t)^*$.
important_parameters: The interaction-to-tunnelling ratio ($V/t$) is the primary varying parameter, with intermediate and large $V/t$ defining distinct physical regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on projecting the dynamics onto manifolds defined by the number of nearest-neighbor bonds ($N_{\mathrm{NN}}$) and considering the effect of transverse confinement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover of $ ar{\eta}$ vs. $V/t$ for different interaction models, showing the transition from delocalizing to localizing behavior, and also plot IPR and hybridization measures ($\Delta\sigma_{NNN}$) across the parameter space.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian, defines key diagnostics ($ ar{\eta}$, IPR), and then explores the non-monotonic dependence of the dynamics on $V/t$, detailing the mechanisms of inter-manifold hybridization (delocalizing) versus intra-manifold degeneracy lifting (localizing).
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical understanding of how long-range, anisotropic interactions can lead to complex, non-monotonic dynamics in quantum many-body systems, which is highly relevant for controlling quantum transport in engineered quantum materials.

Figure 4 shows the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian pro- jected onto the NNN = 4 manifold, P4HP4. In the NN model, all Fock configurations within this manifold have the same interaction energy 4V . The NN interac- tion therefore leaves their degeneracy intact; within the projected Hamiltonian it contributes only an overall en- ergy shift. The corresponding eigenstates consequently remain strongly delocalised in the Fock basis, with low IPR, independently of V/t, as shown in Fig. 4(a). The dipolar tail changes this situation qualitatively. Already its leading contribution, V2NNNN, lifts the degeneracy between Fock configurations with different NNNN. Figure 3(c) shows ∆σNNN for both dipolar interactions. It is positive and maximal at intermediate V/t ∼5, demon- strating that the dipolar tail keeps the state distributed over a broader range of NNN manifolds than in the NN model. At larger V/t, ∆σNNN decreases towards zero as inter-manifold hybridisation becomes suppressed in both models. The confinement-modified dipolar inter- action with βeff = 1.8 produces a larger ∆σNNN, showing that its stronger NNN coupling enhances the delocalising inter-manifold mechanism.
